title: Streets and Squares
objective: After this level you can explain how public squares bring people together.
summary: Siena's Campo was built as a meeting place. Whyte found people sit where there's seating; Jacobs argued busy streets are safe streets; Copenhagen's car-free Strøget (1962) thrived.

cards.headline: Siena paved its main square to point at the government.
cards.body: Siena's Piazza del Campo is shaped like a shell, and its brick paving is divided into nine parts that all point toward the Palazzo Pubblico, the seat of government. What makes a public space pull people in?

cards.headline: A square made for meeting
cards.body: The nine parts recall the Government of the Nine, which ruled Siena from 1287 to 1355. But the Campo was made for everyone: a meeting place for citizens, with markets, games and political events. It still hosts the Palio horse race twice a year. A good square is the town's living room, with the town hall as the armchair everyone faces.

cards.headline: Give people somewhere to sit
cards.body: How do you tell a good plaza from a bad one? William H. Whyte simply watched. Filming New York plazas with time-lapse cameras, he found that "people tend to sit where there are places to sit" (1980). It sounds obvious. It took cameras to prove it: sitting space mattered more than open space. A huge empty plaza loses to a small one with good ledges.

mascot.line: Years of careful filming to prove people like chairs. That's science: check the obvious, find the surprise.

cards.headline: Eyes upon the street
cards.body: In The Death and Life of Great American Cities (1961), Jane Jacobs argued that a well-used street is apt to be a safe one. Her key ingredient: "eyes upon the street," from shops and homes whose windows face it. A blank wall watches nothing. A row of windows is a neighborhood watch that never signs up.

cards.fact: Copenhagen took the cars off its main street in 1962.
cards.context: Strøget was made car-free as an experiment, despite warnings that no cars would mean no customers. According to the Global Designing Cities Initiative, it succeeded and increased revenue for local shops. The street became what Siena's square always was: a place to be, not just a way through.

cards.headline: Streets and squares: gathered
learned: Siena's Campo: nine parts pointing to the town hall
Whyte: people sit where there are places to sit
Jacobs: busy streets with eyes upon them are safer
Strøget went car-free in 1962 and thrived

questions.prompt: What do the nine sections of Siena's Piazza del Campo recall?

options.label: Nine horses in the first Palio
options.rationale: The Palio uses the square; the nine recall a government.

options.label: Nine gates in the city wall
options.rationale: They recall the rulers of 1287 to 1355.

options.label: Nine churches around the square
options.rationale: They point toward the Palazzo Pubblico, the seat of government.

questions.explanation: The nine parts recall the Government of the Nine, which ruled Siena from 1287 to 1355.

questions.prompt: What did William H. Whyte's time-lapse films of New York plazas show?

options.label: People avoid plazas near busy streets
options.rationale: His headline finding was about seating.

options.label: The biggest plazas are always the busiest
options.rationale: Open space alone didn't draw crowds.

options.label: Fountains matter more than anything else
People tend to sit where there are places to sit

questions.explanation: Whyte found that "people tend to sit where there are places to sit": seating, not sheer size, drew people.

questions.prompt: Level 84's Central Park hid its crosstown roads below the landscape. How did Copenhagen's 1962 Strøget experiment deal with cars?

options.label: It took them off the street entirely
It sank them into a tunnel below
options.rationale: That's closer to Central Park's trick.

options.label: It added a lane for them
options.rationale: It went the other way: car-free.

options.label: It charged them a toll at the gates

questions.explanation: Central Park hid traffic out of sight; Strøget simply became a car-free street, and shops did better.
